bio.en: Adam Mosseri is the Head of Instagram, leading a platform used by over three billion people monthly, and previously designed and led the early Facebook News Feed and its ranking algorithm.
bio.zh: Adam Mosseri 是 Instagram 负责人，领导着月活超过 30 亿人的平台，此前曾设计并主导 Facebook 早期动态消息（News Feed）及其排序算法。

summary.en: Adam argues that taste matters more than ever in an AI world where building is cheap, and that the most valuable people will be clear-eyed about what AI is and isn't good at. He explains that the Instagram algorithm understands users far less semantically than people assume, and predicts AI-generated content will ultimately be a tailwind as people seek out authenticity. He also discusses why human judgment remains essential in the product development lifecycle even as AI eats more of it.
summary.zh: Adam 认为，在 AI 让“造东西”变得廉价的时代，品味比以往任何时候都更重要，而最有价值的人是对 AI 擅长与不擅长之处有清醒认知的人。他解释道，Instagram 算法对用户兴趣的理解远比人们想象的更“非语义化”，并预测 AI 生成内容最终会是顺风，因为人们会更渴望真实。他还讨论了为何即便 AI 吞噬更多产品开发环节，人类判断依然不可或缺。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: No, I think taste matters a ton. In a world where it's easier to build things, it's more important to make sure that your time is spent figuring out what you should be building in the first place. The people who I think are going to make the most of it are the ones who are clear-eyed about what AI is good at and what it's not good at, and also have an instinct or a nose for what it will be good at and not good at.
turns.zh: 不，我认为品味非常重要。在一个更容易造东西的世界里，更重要的是确保你的时间花在想清楚你到底该造什么上。我觉得最能从中获益的人，是那些对 AI 擅长什么、不擅长什么有清醒认知，同时对它未来会擅长什么、不擅长什么有直觉和嗅觉的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that the Instagram algorithm knows about human behavior that people may not realize?
turns.zh: Instagram 算法对人类行为有哪些人们可能没意识到的了解？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I think people assume that there's a much more detailed semantic understanding of everybody's interests and preferences in the algorithm than there is.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们以为算法对每个人的兴趣和偏好有非常详细的语义化理解，但实际上并没有那么深。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is the rise of AI content a headwind or a tailwind for Instagram versus other platforms?
turns.zh: AI 内容的崛起对 Instagram 相对其他平台来说是逆风还是顺风？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I think it's going to be a tailwind, but I think it's going to be a challenge. In a world where there's an abundance of synthetic content, I actually think people are going to seek out creativity and authenticity and people. I don't think we should filter out AI content. I think we should let you know if content is AI content or not. That's hard, by the way.
turns.zh: 我觉得会是顺风，但也会是个挑战。在一个合成内容泛滥的世界里，我反而觉得人们会更去寻找创意、真实性和人。我不认为我们应该过滤掉 AI 内容。我认为我们应该让你知道内容是不是 AI 生成的。这很难做到，顺便说一句。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where do you think human brains will continue to be most valuable as AI continues to eat more and more of that product development life cycle?
turns.zh: 随着 AI 继续吃掉越来越多的产品开发生命周期，你觉得人类大脑在哪里会继续最有价值？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: That's a great question, so-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been doing product for a long time. You get to see how a lot of teams operate across Meta, within Instagram. What does just the canonical product team look like in 2026? What's kind of most different today in how teams operate/should operate versus, say, a couple years ago?
turns.zh: 你做产品很久了。你能看到 Meta 旗下、Instagram 内部很多团队是怎么运作的。2026 年标准的产品团队长什么样？和几年前相比，今天团队的运作方式有什么最大的不同？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: It's changed a lot this year. So for the longest time at a big company like ours, the canonical team was something like two or three Android engineers, two or three iOS engineers, two or three server engineers, maybe a generalist, a PM, a designer, a data scientist, a researcher, if you were lucky, and maybe that's about it. So on the order of a Baker's dozen. And that is a function of you want to have, for anybody who's running code, someone who can review their code and who's familiar with that code base, and having these different functions that are more specialized. I think it's very different at a startup. (00:03:14): But this year, it's changing. We've adopted what we call pods, which are just mini teams, where it's, call it, four to six engineers who are a bit more generalists. One, we call product staff, which is sort of an evolution of the PM, so a PM who can do some of what a designer does, and some of what a data scientist does, and some of what a research does, leveraging the latest tools that we have for them. And then whatever specialist they need. If they're doing something that requires a pricing strategy, you need a senior data scientist. If you're doing something that is really novel from an experience standpoint, you need a very senior product designer. (00:03:57): So we try to build a team based on the needs of the work a bit, but then end up with a much smaller core, which is more on the order of six or seven usually. And that is a very big shift that's just happening to us this year. But just by virtue of having less people to coordinate, they can often move faster and make better decisions, a little bit less designed by committee. So we talk a lot about AI adjusting and improving productivity, and that's part of it. But I think another part of it is just the small teams, I think, often are just more effective.
turns.zh: 今年变化很大。很久以来，在像我们这样的大公司，标准团队大概是这样：两三个 Android 工程师、两三个 iOS 工程师、两三个服务端工程师，可能再加个全栈，一个 PM、一个设计师、一个数据科学家，运气好的话还有一个研究员，大概就这样。差不多十几个人。这是因为你要确保每个写代码的人都有人 review、熟悉同一套代码库，还有这些更专业化的不同职能。我觉得创业公司很不一样。(00:03:14)：但今年在变。我们采用了叫 pod 的模式，就是小团队，大概四到六个更偏全栈的工程师。一个我们叫 product staff 的角色，是 PM 的进化版——一个能做部分设计师工作、部分数据科学家工作、部分研究员工作的 PM，借助我们最新的工具。然后是按需的专家。如果做需要定价策略的事，你需要一个资深数据科学家。如果做体验上非常新颖的事，你需要一个非常资深的产品设计师。(00:03:57)：所以我们尝试根据工作需要来组建团队，最终核心团队通常只有六七个人。这是今年正在发生的很大转变。但仅仅因为需要协调的人少了，他们通常能更快地推进、做出更好的决策，更少「委员会设计」。所以大家聊很多 AI 提升生产力，这是其中一部分。但另一部分就是小团队往往就是更高效。

turns.en: You just have less specialists, right? So you might not have any. You might be four engineers and a product staff, and there's no data scientist, there's no designer, there's no researcher, there's no content designer. The product staff is the generalist that supports all of those things. (00:06:14): I mean, what's clearly happening is all of the functions are starting to bleed into each other, and the whole industry's wrestling with what that means. A lot of what a data scientist does at a big company, for instance, is relatively mechanical. And so there's stuff that they do that is really more like art and science and there's stuff that's really more like just pulling data, data management. (00:06:37): So some of the tools that we're building internally to understand ... For instance, a traditional data science question would be a waterfall. So if you wanted to look at people creating reels, you would look at all the steps and then how people fall off on each step, and try to figure out where there might be opportunities to improve things. That kind of basic waterfall analysis is much easier now to use some of our internal tools to just pull automatically, as opposed to having to have a data scientist do a bunch of bespoke work for that. So our product staff might be able to do that now, and they couldn't do that a year ago. (00:07:11): So you just end up with these people who have more generalist shapes. turns.zh: 你就是专家少了。可能一个都没有。可能是四个工程师加一个 product staff，没有数据科学家、没有设计师、没有研究员、没有内容设计师。product staff 就是支撑所有这些职能的全才。(00:06:14)：我的意思是，正在发生的是所有职能开始互相渗透，整个行业都在纠结这意味着什么。比如大公司里数据科学家做的很多事是相对机械的。他们做的一些事确实更像艺术和科学，但也有一些就是拉数据、数据管理。(00:06:37)：所以我们内部构建的一些工具来理解……比如一个传统的数据科学问题是漏斗分析。如果你想看用户创建 Reels 的流程，你会看所有步骤以及每一步的流失，试图找出改进机会。这种基础漏斗分析现在用我们的一些内部工具可以自动拉出来，不需要数据科学家做一堆定制工作。所以我们的 product staff 现在做得了这个，而一年前做不了。(00:07:11)：所以你最终会得到这些更全栈的人。然后当你真正需要时，你会有更资深的、或更有创造力的专家。比如一个 phenomenal 的产品设计师，或者一个天才数据科学家或研究员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. It's exactly what I just heard. I had Fiona Fong, the head of engineering for Claude Code and co-work on the podcast. She's Boris Cherry's manager, and she described the people she hires now are, one, builders with great taste that can take an idea from end-to-end, and people with deep expertise in a very specific domain.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。和我刚听到的完全一样。我之前请了 Fiona Fong，她是 Claude Code 的工程负责人，Boris Cherry 的 manager。她描述她现在招的人，一是能端到端把想法落地的有品味的 builder，二是在某个非常具体领域有深度专长的人。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: The taste thing matters a lot. I really agree with that. Boris used to work at Instagram.
turns.zh: 品味这件事很重要。我非常同意。Boris 之前在 Instagram 工作过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, that's right.
turns.zh: 哦对。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, he was a senior IC at Instagram for a while. I love seeing him. He's all over Threads now. It's like he's sort of like the face of Claude Code, which is amazing. Yeah, he's crushing it.
turns.zh: 对，他在 Instagram 做过一段时间资深 IC。我很高兴看到他现在在 Threads 上到处活跃。他简直就是 Claude Code 的代言人，太棒了。他做得非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's killing it. He's a celebrity now.
turns.zh: 他太厉害了。他现在是名人了。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: He really is. He's his own little ... Yeah, for sure. In a world that is on fire right now. No, I think taste matters a ton. So in a world where it's easier to build things, it's more important to make sure that your time is spent figuring out what you should be building in the first place. (00:08:28): Actually, so a lot of designers right now are very anxious about their roles. You know, I've got these other generalists doing design, you've got engineers doing design, product staff doing design. But I'm actually pretty long on design or designers because they tend to have taste. And I think that is something that is much more difficult to imagine being automated away. And so there's other challenges with design sometimes, but I'm pretty long right now on designers.
turns.zh: 他真的是。他有自己的……对，肯定。在一个当下火热的世界里。不，我觉得品味非常重要。在一个更容易造东西的世界里，更重要的是确保时间花在想清楚到底该造什么上。(00:08:28)：其实现在很多设计师对自己的角色很焦虑——有别的全才在做设计、工程师在做设计、product staff 在做设计。但我其实很看好设计师，因为他们通常有品味。我觉得这是很难想象被自动化的东西。设计有它自己的挑战，但我现在对设计师是看多的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've always felt that too. As it is so easy to build and all the work that AI produces is so ... You can tell this was Claude designed. I know what you did here. This is Codex.
turns.zh: 我一直也这么觉得。当造东西变得这么容易，AI 产出的所有东西又都那么……你能看出来这是 Claude 设计的。我知道你这里做了什么。这是 Codex。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Well, they all have their vibe. When you vibe code your apps, we call it vibe coding, and you're all like, "Oh, that's a Codex app," or, "Oh, that's a Claude app."
turns.zh: 嗯，它们都有自己的 vibe。当你 vibe code 你的应用时，我们叫它 vibe coding，你就会「哦，这是个 Codex 应用」「哦，这是个 Claude 应用」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. And that's Replate, that's Lovable. You can predict these things. I've always though that too, that design should be thriving, or, you know, for some reason, it hasn't yet. If you look at jobs for designers, they're kind of flat lining. I feel like the missing piece is like the PME piece of deeply understanding the business, and what will grow it, and what success, you know, all that stuff. The business side of it versus the taste side of it.
turns.zh: 对。那是 Replate，那是 Lovable。你能预测这些。我一直也这么觉得，设计应该是蓬勃发展的，但出于某种原因，还没有。如果你看设计师的招聘，基本是平的。我觉得缺失的那块是 PM 那种深入理解业务、什么能增长它、成功是什么的那一面。业务面而非品味面。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. I think you're going to see ... We have a senior designer at Instagram called Nate, who just transferred into product staff. So I think some of what you'll see is it will be harder to talk about design roles and who's a good designer because they're not going to just stay in traditional design roles. If you're an amazing designer, you probably have strong opinions outside of just the interaction and visual design. You probably have strong opinions on product strategy, even on the business, on the go-to-market. (00:10:13): And so I actually think some of our strongest product staff are going to be converts from design and from data science who are just looking to expand their reach. And they were influential across functional boundaries before, but this world where those functional boundaries are just wildly blurred, just allow them just to jump in. And so sure, they'll be technically a generalist on paper, but they clearly have a uniquely strong ability in one type of craft. But they've got the ability and strong opinions to make informed decisions across other parts or other crafts. (00:10:46): And so I don't know that all the strongest designers I have will all be in design. They probably will be the majority, but I can imagine a bunch of really strong ones moving roles. But, I mean, I should also check my own bias here though, because I started as a designer at Facebook way back when, and I switched roles.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得你会看到……Instagram 有个资深设计师叫 Nate，刚转成 product staff。所以我觉得你会看到的是，谈论设计角色和谁是好的设计师会变得更难，因为他们不会只待在传统设计角色里。如果你是个出色的设计师，你大概在交互和视觉设计之外也有强观点——对产品策略、甚至业务、go-to-market 都有。(00:10:13)：所以我其实觉得我们最强的一些 product staff 会是从设计和数据科学转过来的，他们就是想扩大自己的影响范围。他们之前就在跨职能边界上有影响力，但在这个职能边界模糊的世界里，他们可以直接跳进去。所以当然，纸面上他们是全才，但他们在某一种 craft 上有独特强项。同时他们有能力、有强观点去在其他部分做出明智决策。(00:10:46)：所以我不觉得我所有最强的设计师都会在设计岗上。可能大多数会，但我能想象一些很强的人转岗。不过我也得检视自己的偏见，因为我当年就是以设计师身份加入 Facebook 的，后来转了岗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, designers are great. I'm a big fan. So this is really interesting. There's always been this GM model where different types of functions can become GMs. It's like this product staff role feels like a similar situation, where different functions can become product staff.
turns.zh: 不，设计师很棒。我是大粉丝。这真有意思。一直有 GM 模式，不同职能可以成为 GM。这个 product staff 角色感觉是类似的情况，不同职能可以成为 product staff。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And that was true of PM before, but it's just so much more true now. And, I mean, in some ways, it's probably the age of the generalist, but I still think there's going to be a real important role for these really amazing specialists who are just ... They're all about going ... I wish I was like that. I always had this, like I romanticize the phenomenal machine learning engineer or AI researcher or shoemaker. I think that's the coolest thing in the world. But it's never been my shape. I've never been great at anything. I've always just had range. That's always been my strength.
turns.zh: 对。对。PM 以前就是这样，但现在更是如此。在某种程度上，这可能是全才的时代，但我仍然觉得那些真正厉害的专家会有非常重要的角色——他们就是那种……我wish自己是那样。我总是浪漫化那种 phenomenal 的机器学习工程师、AI 研究员或 shoemaker。我觉得那是世界上最酷的事。但这从来不是我的形状。我什么都不精通，我一直都是有 range，这直是我的优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same. Okay. So this idea of product staff. So the idea is on these new pods ... So this is a new thing you guys are doing. So there's these pod teams, product staff, engineers, and maybe one specialist that's going deep on set pricing algorithm or something like that. So what this tells me is there's these adjacent roles that are maybe more in trouble over the years. Data science, for example, user research, for example. You talked about designers being anxious. Is there anything there of just like, "Oh, maybe folks in these groups should think about shifting to other roles."?
turns.zh: 一样。好的。这个 product staff 的想法。所以这些新 pod 上……这是你们在做的新事。有 pod 团队、product staff、工程师，可能还有一个深入做定价算法之类的专家。这告诉我的是，有些相邻角色未来几年可能更危险。比如数据科学、用户研究。你谈到设计师焦虑。有没有什么想法，比如这些群体的人是不是该考虑转岗？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I mean, there's anxiety everywhere. I mean, I've talked to a lot of people at a lot of other companies, and it just seems like this is a lot of concern right now about competition, about job displacement, about unintended or unforeseen consequences of all this technology and all this moving so quickly. So that's definitely happening. (00:12:44): I think that you will see the functional lines continue to blur, but I still think there will be room for functions. They'll just be shaped differently. They won't all be senior ICs necessarily, but they'll all be either senior or on their way to being senior. You can't just have a bunch of super senior data scientists and no new ones, because then who's going to be the new super senior data scientists in the future? So you need to basically hire and mentor and grow talent. Maybe the team is smaller overall, and then that those who aren't on their way to being super senior move into more of a generalist role. I think that's a reasonable soft landing. But I do think you're going to want to make sure you're investing not only in today's senior talent for each specific function, but in tomorrow's. Otherwise, I think you're going to regret it in a couple years is my take. (00:13:36): That said, who knows what the world looks like in a couple of years? So my big thing is generally don't be overly confident in whatever your predictions are, because there's just too much flux right now.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，到处都有焦虑。我聊了很多其他公司的人，现在对竞争、对工作被替代、对所有这些技术快速移动的意外后果，都有很多担忧。这确实在发生。(00:12:44)：我觉得你会看到职能边界继续模糊，但我仍然觉得会有职能的空间，只是形状不同。他们不一定都是资深 IC，但都会是资深或正在走向资深的人。你不能只有一堆超级资深的数据科学家而没有新人，否则未来谁来当超级资深数据科学家？所以你需要招人、带人、培养人才。也许团队整体更小，那些没在走向超级资深的人转成更全才的角色。我觉得这是个合理的软着陆。但我确实觉得你要确保不仅投资今天的资深人才，也要投资明天的。否则几年后你会后悔。(00:13:36)：话虽如此，谁知道几年后世界什么样？所以我的大原则是别对自己的预测过度自信，因为现在变化太多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Benedict Evans was on the podcast recently, said the same thing, "We don't want to know anything about what's going on."
turns.zh: Benedict Evans 最近上过播客，说的也是这个：「我们不想对正在发生的事做任何判断。」

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I like him a lot. I'll make sure I listen to the pod.
turns.zh: 对，对。我很喜欢他。我一定去听听那期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So you talked about taste. This makes me think about ... So you're interviewing a lot of people, hiring a lot of people. What are some traits that are trending up in things that you look for more and more now in this world? And what are some traits that are trending down, and maybe less important to you?
turns.zh: 好。你谈到了品味。这让我想到……你在面试很多人、招很多人。在这个世界里，有哪些特质是你越来越看重的、呈上升趋势的？又有哪些在下降、对你不那么重要了？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I mean, there are some things that are the same. So for the longest time, almost no matter what the function, I always look for three things. Do you have sort of grit? You've got some drive, some fire in your belly. Are you a quick learner? And are you reasonably ideally very self-aware so that you can actually take feedback and know what you're good at and know you're not good? Because if you are those things, if you got fire in your belly, you learn quickly and you're self-aware, you can kind of get good at anything eventually. But if any of those things are missing, there's usually an issue, so that's the baseline. (00:14:53): Right now for hiring, but just for I think people who are going to be more successful over these next 5 or 10 years, as things change so significantly, I think two things that I'm continuing to encourage myself to do, are to stay curious and to put yourself out there. I just think you got to try things. To that point before where no one really knows what's going on, you have to be willing to try things. I don't know, do you speak another language?
turns.zh: 有些东西是不变的。很久以来，不管什么职能，我始终看三点：你有没有韧性？有没有驱动力、肚子里的火？你是不是学得快？你够不够——理想是非常——有自我意识，能真正接受反馈、知道自己擅长什么不擅长什么？因为如果你有这些，你能慢慢擅长任何事。但如果缺了任何一个，通常就会有问题。这是基线。(00:14:53)：现在招人，或者说在未来 5 到 10 年随着事情剧变更成功的人，我持续鼓励自己做的两件事是：保持好奇和把自己推出去。我觉得你就是得去试。回到刚才说的，没人真知道会发生什么，你得愿意去试。你会说另一种语言吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Russian, yeah.
turns.zh: 俄语，对。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. So when you learn another language, I think one of the most important things and one of the best predictors, this is my guess, I don't have any research on this, about are you going to get good at speaking, is are you willing to sound like an idiot? Are you willing just to say it and be corrected, and not be offended, and then just get better and better? You just have to put yourself out there. (00:15:44): And with all of these new tools and models and technologies, I think you just have to be willing to try stuff. So if you're curious when you try stuff, I think that you'll learn, you'll adapt. But if you're not curious or you're not willing to make mistakes or try things, I think you're in a ton of trouble, or at least I think it's going to be a really difficult time. So those, I think, are premiums, not just for hiring at a company like Meta or a team like Instagram, but I just think across the industry, and multiple industries over the next 10 to 20 years. (00:16:12): Is this something that maybe we're looking for less of? For some of these functions, I think that there's some that are still going to be very large teams, and so you need people who are really good at managing large organizations. Large organizational leadership is its own craft and skill. It's actually different than management. But I do think there'll be less of those roles. I think we'll have more smaller teams, and there'll be less people who manage thousands of people. And so that's not that job will go away, but that will be less of what I'm looking for in hires, because I'm going to have less roles like that.
turns.zh: 对。学另一种语言时，我觉得最重要也最好的预测——这是我猜的，没研究——你能不能学好口语，就是你愿不愿意听起来像个傻瓜？愿不愿意就这么说、被纠正、不觉得被冒犯，然后越来越好？你就是得把自己推出去。(00:15:44)：面对所有这些新工具、模型、技术，我觉得你得愿意去试。如果你保持好奇去试，你会学到、会适应。但如果你不好奇或不愿犯错、不愿尝试，我觉得你会有大麻烦，至少会非常艰难。所以这些是 premium，不仅是对 Meta 或 Instagram 招人，我觉得是跨行业、未来 10 到 20 年的。(00:16:12)：什么是我们可能没那么看重的？对于一些职能，有些还是会有很大团队，所以你需要擅长管理大组织的人。大组织领导力是一门独立的 craft 和技能，和管理不同。但我确实觉得这类角色会更少。我们会有更多小团队，管几千人的人会更少。所以那个工作不会消失，但会少。我招人时对这类角色的需求会少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I'm hearing from a few folks is AI is almost kind of resetting people's impact and success, in terms of some people that were maybe low performers pre-AI can now do ... Like things they were bad at, AI now allows them to do. And now they're thriving, building all these things, helping other people. Do you see that at all? Just AI is just lifting other people up, maybe lowering some people down?
turns.zh: 我从几个人那里听到的是，AI 几乎在重置人们的影响力和成功。一些 AI 之前的低绩效者现在能做……他们以前不擅长的事 AI 让他们能做了。现在他们蓬勃发展，建各种东西、帮别人。你看到这个了吗？AI 就是在把一些人托起来，也许同时把一些人压下去？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, I mean the job is just different. Take engineering. Engineering used to be, maybe not majority, but a large percentage, 40%, 50%, 60% writing code. It's not now, especially if you talk to anybody at these labs. They're spending most of their time planning and reviewing code. That is a very different job. You might hate that, and you might have loved just writing code. Or you might love that, and you might not have been that fast at writing code. So who succeeds is a function of whose strengths are aligned with the tools' needs and the business' needs. And so this is definitely happening. (00:17:54): Another thing is you've had people who had good ideas about how to contribute it to other functions, but didn't have the mechanical or technical skills to do so. And AI reduces the boundary to do that, and then all of a sudden they can. (00:18:11): For me, it's kind of funny because when I got hired at Facebook, all the designers had to be able to program. I went through a technical loop. We gave up on that because it was too hard to hire people. But I now get to program again for the first time in maybe 10 years. And, you know, I am not a good engineer. I'm a mediocre engineer on a good day. But now, I can write code responsibly, which is just an amazing thing. You're seeing this across all sorts of levels in seniority and functions. Designers who are programming, engineers who are pulling data and doing strong analyses, data scientists who are putting together proposals for designs. (00:18:56): The tools aren't all great, by the way. I think too often we have this really polarized binary outlook on the state of AI. Like, are you AI-pilled or are you anti-AI? It's like, people are binary. I said that to the team yesterday. And the state of the tools isn't binary either. They're amazing at some things and remarkably bad at others. And the people who I think are going to make the most of it are the ones who are clear-eyed about what AI is good at and what it's not good at, and also have an instinct or a nose for what it will be good at and not good at next month or in a couple months from now.
turns.zh: 对，工作就是不一样了。拿工程来说。以前工程——可能不是大部分，但很大比例，40%、50%、60%——是写代码。现在不是了，尤其是你跟这些实验室的人聊。他们大部分时间在规划和 review 代码。这是非常不同的工作。你可能讨厌这个，可能之前就是爱写代码。或者你可能爱这个，之前写代码没那么快。所以谁成功取决于谁的优势和工具、业务需求对齐。这确实在发生。(00:17:54)：另一件事是，有些人对其他职能怎么贡献有好想法，但没机械或技术能力去做。AI 降低了这个门槛，突然他们就能做了。(00:18:11)：对我来说挺有趣，因为我入职 Facebook 时，所有设计师都必须能编程。我经历了技术面。后来我们放弃了这个要求因为太难招人了。但我现在又能编程了，这是十年来第一次。我不是好工程师，好日子也就中等水平。但现在我能负责任地写代码，这太棒了。你在各种层级和职能都看到这个：设计师在编程、工程师在拉数据做扎实分析、数据科学家在出设计方案。(00:18:56)：顺便说一句，工具不是都好。我觉得太经常我们对 AI 的状态有非常极化的二元看法——你是 AI 派还是反 AI 派？人就是二元的。我昨天跟团队这么说。工具的状态也不是二元的。它们有些事惊人地好，有些事出奇地差。我觉得最能从中获益的人，是那些对 AI 擅长什么、不擅长什么有清醒认知的人……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned that AI writes all our code now. Someone tweeted this idea that stuck with me for months now of just like, "Remember, we used to be able to just write code for free?"
turns.zh: 你说到 AI 现在写我们所有的代码。有人发推一个想法，困扰了我好几个月：「记得我们以前能免费写代码吗？」

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I think you'll still be able to write code for free, it'll just be with a smaller model, but yes. That is [inaudible 00:19:58].
turns.zh: 我觉得你还是能免费写代码，只是用更小的模型，但没错。这确实[听不清 00:19:58]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess that's true. There's a model that are close to free, but it's like, yeah, that's crazy. Now it's just like totally-
turns.zh: 我想也是。有些模型接近免费，但就是，对，这太疯狂了。现在完全——

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: But just think about the cost, think about what you pay for a model now and what the level of intelligence you're getting from that model is. And then at that same price point a year ago, what were you getting? At some point, the incremental value won't matter. We're getting there I think with small projects and programming. I think the models will matter even beyond ... This week you've got Fable and, obviously, Mythos from Anthropic, but I spent a lot of time with that this week. For the first time, I'm like, "Oh, I'm just talking to a much more technical, much smarter engineer than I am." The next version, a year out, of that model, do I need to pay for frontier tokens for whatever Anthropic model 6.0 is? Or is Fable just fine for all of my side projects? Probably just fine. Probably pretty cheap by then too.
turns.zh: 但想想成本，想想你现在为一个模型付多少钱、得到什么水平的智能。一年前同样的价位你得到什么？到某个点，增量价值就不重要了。我觉得小程序和编程上快到了。我觉得模型会一直重要……这周有 Fable 和 Anthropic 的 Mythos，我这周花了很多时间在上面。第一次我觉得：「哦，我就是在和一个比我技术强得多、聪明得多的工程师说话。」下个版本，一年后，我还需要为 Anthropic 6.0 之类的前沿模型付 frontier token 费吗？还是 Fable 就够我所有副业项目用了？可能就够了。到时候可能也很便宜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. When Kevin Weil on the podcast when he was CPO at OpenAI, he famously said, "This is the worst the model will ever be." It's still hard to comprehend that. It's only going to get better. So on this point of tokens, spend, ROI, and things like that, Meta is famous for this leaderboard of token spend.
turns.zh: 对。Kevin Weil 上播客时还是 OpenAI 的 CPO，他有句名言：「这是模型有史以来最差的时候。」仍然很难理解。它只会更好。所以关于 token、花费、ROI 这些，Meta 以 token 花费排行榜出名。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: It's a terrible idea. No leaderboards for token spend.
turns.zh: 那是糟主意。不要 token 花费排行榜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay. Talk about that, and just how do you think about just budgets for engineers and product teams at this point? Just spend as much as you want? Is it like there's a cap we have? Is there any sort of thing you've figured out that works well?
turns.zh: 好的。好的。聊聊这个，你现在怎么想工程师和产品团队的预算？想花多少花多少？还是有上限？有没有什么你觉得有效的方式？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Right now, we've managed to get the costs reigned in a little bit by shutting down the silly things that we were doing. It's not that hard to build a token incinerator and that doesn't create a lot of value. And as soon as you actually look at the dollars in and value out, you might just be like, "Oh, that's just a bad idea." And so right now, we don't have token limits for our engineers. Actually, I think for anybody, really. I think that'll eventually have to happen, particularly if costs go up before they go down. I think they'll eventually go down for the reasons that we just talked about. (00:22:12): But I think of it as any other resource, like I have to decide how to deploy capacity to my different teams, because I have a limited number of GPUs and CPUs and storage and RAM, et cetera. I have to decide how to deploy OPEX for labeling budgets across my teams. I have to decide how to deploy payroll for headcount across my teams. I think that you can imagine, at least in a year or two coming, that the burn rate of a strong engineer might be the same as their salary or their cost of employment. And in that world, you're going to probably need to put in some caps. The caps should probably be portional to the company's trust in your ability to use them in an ROA positive way. But I can imagine caps being healthy. Right now, we're not there. (00:23:07): I think costs will go up because we'll just be using more tokens, not because prices will necessarily go up. But then I think prices will come down because all of these frontier models are going to be in a bit of a pricing war. So we'll see. I think it'll be a bit of a rollercoaster.
turns.zh: 现在，我们通过停掉一些 silly 的做法把成本控制住了一些。建一个 token 焚烧炉不难，但它创造不了多少价值。一旦你看投入的钱和产出的价值，你就会「哦，这主意不好」。所以现在我们没给工程师设 token 限制。其实我觉得对任何人都没有。我觉得最终得有，特别是如果成本先涨后降的话。我觉得成本最终会降，原因就是我们刚说的。(00:22:12)：但我把它当成任何其他资源，比如我得决定把算力分给哪些团队——GPU、CPU、存储、内存是有限的。我得决定标注预算怎么分。我得决定 headcount 薪酬怎么分。你能想象一两年后，一个强工程师的 burn rate 可能和他的薪水一样高。到那时你可能得设上限。上限大概应该和公司对你用它产生正 ROI 的信任成正比。但我能想象设上限是健康的。现在还没到。(00:23:07)：我觉得成本会涨，因为我们用的 token 更多，不是因为价格涨。但之后我觉得价格会降，因为所有前沿模型会打价格战。我们走着瞧。会是个过山车。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So coming back to this idea that, as you said, we've evolved from, we used to write all our code, to now we're approaching all code will be written by AI. And it feels like now the transition is it's not just written by AI, but it's one-shotted by AI. Coding now is steering AI, and it's like how often you have to correct it is coding now. So it's like the software development lifecycle slowly being eaten by AI. It'll start helping us come up with ideas, I imagine, more and more. The question I like to ask people is, where do you think human brains will continue to be most valuable as AI continues to eat more and more of that product development lifecycle?
turns.zh: 回到你说的，我们从自己写所有代码，到现在 AI 写所有代码。感觉现在不只是 AI 写，而是 AI 一次性搞定。现在编程就是引导 AI，你要纠正多少次就是编程。软件开发生命周期正在被 AI 慢慢吃掉。它接下来会帮我们想点子。我喜欢问人的问题是：随着 AI 继续吃掉更多产品开发生命周期，人类大脑在哪里会继续最有价值？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Taste, like we talked about. Judgment, particularly around strategy. You might get feedback from an AI on a strategy, but you're not asking an AI to come up with a strategy anytime soon. Or if you are, then it's within the context of bounds you set. So here's my goal, here's my vision, here are my constraints, here's my job, here's my budget. (00:24:27): I think that it looks more like management. You are trying to define what success looks like, decide how prescriptive you want to be about the path to success, and then giving feedback along the way. And that is its own craft. And it'll be interesting to see how if some of the same dynamics come up. I believe that if you are too prescriptive, as a leader with a team, you end up stifling good ideas. But if you're too open-ended, sometimes teams just waste time going in the wrong direction. And so that level of autonomy you give a team, maybe that applies to agents in the future, particularly when we're talking not just about building something, but deciding what you build in the first place. (00:25:18): But I think of vision as an articulation of the world or the state of the product you want to get to. And I think of strategy as an opinionated path to achieve that vision. Strategy can't be like be the best or be amazing. It has to be controversial, that you have to be ... A reasonable person should be able to disagree with it, because otherwise you're probably just trying to compete on raw execution. And I think both vision and strategy I think are going to be where our brains are spreading more and more of our cycles, and I think less on execution.
turns.zh: 品味，我们说过了。判断力，特别是策略上的。你可能从 AI 得到策略反馈，但你不会很快让 AI 来出策略。或者如果你在这么做，也是在你设定的边界内——这是我的目标、愿景、约束、工作、预算。(00:24:27)：我觉得这更像管理。你在定义成功长什么样，决定对路径要多指令性，然后一路给反馈。这是一门 craft。会很有意思看一些相同 dynamics 是否出现。我相信如果你太指令性，作为 leader 你会扼杀好想法。但太开放，团队有时会浪费时间走错方向。所以你给团队的自主度，也许未来也适用于 agent，特别是不只是造东西、而是决定造什么的时候。(00:25:18)：我把愿景看作对你想到达的世界或产品状态的表达。策略是一个有观点的、实现愿景的路径。策略不能是「做最好」或「做最棒」。它得有争议性，得是——一个理性的人应该能不同意它，否则你大概只是在拼执行。我觉得愿景和策略是我们大脑会花越来越多 cycles 的地方，执行上会少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I have always though is AI should be incredibly good at strategy because you would think, here's the market, here's all the information on the market, our competitors, our metrics, our numbers, our growth, all these things. Help me figure out how to win. You think AI, knowing all that, would be really good at this.
turns.zh: 我一直觉得 AI 应该非常擅长策略，因为你会想：这是市场，这是所有市场信息、竞争对手、指标、数字、增长。帮我搞清楚怎么赢。你觉得 AI 知道这些，应该很擅长这个。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I think it could be. I have found it's not unless you steer it pretty aggressively. And I don't mean towards an answer, I mean based on the constraints. It turns out when you're trying to come up with a strategy, there's a lot of things to consider. You need to consider the state of the technology, personnel on the team and what's motivating them and what you can get. Sometimes coming up with an idea that is on the bubble, you know it's going to actually attract some of the best talent. And so the push then goes to the idea. (00:26:43): Obviously, the competitive landscape, the regulatory landscape for companies as large as ours and the compliance landscape, the identity and reason to exist for the brand, you have to consider all of these things. I think if you ask an AI just for a strategy lazily, you're not going to get something great. You're going to get something pretty predictable that probably the competition would expect you to do. (00:27:08): I think if you want a really more effective one, you need to think long and hard about what are all of the different inputs that need to be considered, make sure you steer the AI in a way that it's considering those as well. And then it needs to be a conversation in the back and forth. But I think if you're willing to put in the work and the time, it can definitely be helpful and definitely be clarifying, particularly if you tell it to be critical. Different models have very different vibes, though, on how willing they are to be pushed back, so I recommend picking one that likes pushing back.
turns.zh: 我觉得它可以。但我发现除非你非常积极地引导，否则它不行。我不是说引导向某个答案，而是基于约束。做策略时要考虑很多。技术状态、团队的人、什么激励他们、你能拿到什么。有时一个刚好在临界点上的 idea 你知道它能吸引最顶尖的人才。所以推力就到了 idea 上。(00:26:43)：当然还有竞争格局、像我们这种公司的监管和合规格局、品牌的身份和存在理由，所有这些都要考虑。我觉得如果你懒洋洋地问 AI 要策略，你不会得到好东西。你会得到相当可预测的、竞争对手大概也猜得到你会做的事。(00:27:08)：如果你想要更有效的策略，你需要认真想清楚所有要考虑的输入，确保 AI 也在考虑这些。然后得是对话、来回。但如果你愿意投入时间和工作，它确实能帮忙、能帮你厘清，特别是你让它批判性。不同模型在愿不愿意 push back 上有很不同的 vibe，我推荐选一个喜欢 push back 的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Mythos has gotten really good at being like, "I can't do this. Let's move on." There's all these limitations.
turns.zh: 对。Mythos 已经很擅长说「我做不了这个。我们继续吧。」有各种限制。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Claude has always been a little bit of a jerk in a way that I actually appreciate. I appreciate it, I really do, because I don't want one that's just like, "Oh, you're so right. I'm so sorry I said that." It's like, no, no, hold on. I want the real intelligence. I don't want the pleaser.
turns.zh: Claude 一直有点像个 jerk，这我很 appreciate。我 appreciate，真的，因为我不想要一个「哦你说得太对了，抱歉我那么说」的。不不不，等等。我要真正的智能。我不要讨好型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point you made about people being excited about the strategy is such an interesting one. There's this idea that I read, I think Cory Doctorow wrote this. There's this kind of concept of a centaur and a reverse centaur. So centaur is a human body horse ... This is going somewhere, I promise. Human body horse ... Sorry, human upper part, horse, lower part.
turns.zh: 你说的关于人们对策略兴奋这一点非常有意思。有个概念我读到过，我想是 Cory Doctorow 写的。就是 centaur 和 reverse centaur 的概念。centaur 是人马……这会绕回来的，我保证。人身马……抱歉，人的上半身，马的下半身。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Horse body. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 马身。对对对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Horse body, where the human is in charge. And we prefer that we want to be in charge. Reverse centaur, which is what we want to avoid with AI, is where the AI is controlling us, and we're just doing its bidding.
turns.zh: 马身，人在主导。我们更喜欢这样，我们想主导。reverse centaur 是我们要避免的 AI 状态——AI 在控制我们，我们只是执行它的指令。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: So it's a horse head on a human body.
turns.zh: 所以是马头人身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: It's terrifying.
turns.zh: 那太可怕了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in a sense, Uber drivers and DoorDash people, this is their life, which is not great. And this is the danger, I think, for a lot of people is if it's giving us the strategy and telling us, "Here's what we're building" No one's going to want to do that. So that's a really interesting counterpoint to, we don't want AI to be telling us the strategy, almost.
turns.zh: 某种意义上，Uber 司机和 DoorDash 骑手的生活就是这样，不太好。我觉得这对很多人来说也是危险——如果是 AI 给我们策略、告诉我们「这是我们要造的」，没人会想做。所以这是个很有意思的反论点：我们几乎不想让 AI 来定策略。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, no, I think there's a lot of things to be careful about right now. And I would certainly not just assume that because you might be able to outsource some workflow to AI, that you should. There are certain ones where I think it's really just a win-win and there are certain ones where I think the risk outweighs the benefits.
turns.zh: 对，不，我觉得现在有很多要小心的事。我当然不会仅仅因为你可以把某个流程外包给 AI，就认为你应该。有些确实是双赢，有些风险大于收益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Mercury. Radically different banking loved by over 300,000 entrepreneurs, and now with Command. I've been a customer of Mercury's for over six years. I have never once though about leaving. Mercury is basically what happens when banking is built by product people, not by bankers. They make it so easy, dare I say fun, to send invoices, move money around, set up virtual cards for folks on my team. Does your bank have an API, a terminal native CLI or an AI-ready MCP server? I don't think so. (00:29:57): And just recently, they launched Command, a conversational interface built directly into Mercury, which acts as your financial operator. I've been using Command to transfer money around, to figure out what categories I've been spending the most money in, analyze my cash flows. And just today, I used it to find out how much I've made from a specific sponsor over the past year. I just ask, "How much have I made from X over the past year?" 10 seconds later, I have an answer. It is so freaking cool. Visit mercury.com to learn more, and apply online in minutes. Mercury is a FinTech company, not an FDIC-insured bank. Banking services provided through Choice Financial Group and Column N.A., Members FDIC. (00:30:37): Okay, going back to product leadership, things you've learned along your journey, we were chatting ahead of this about just things you've learned, and one thing that you said about some of the best product leaders you've worked with is that they're less visionary and more curators. I'd love to hear more along these lines.
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Mercury 赞助。被超过 30 万创业者喜爱的截然不同的银行，现在还有 Command。我用 Mercury 超过六年了，从没想过离开。Mercury 基本上就是产品人做的银行，不是银行家做的银行。他们让发发票、转账、给团队设虚拟卡变得超简单，甚至可以说有趣。你的银行有 API、terminal 原生 CLI 或 AI-ready MCP server 吗？我猜没有。(00:29:57)：最近他们上线了 Command，直接内置在 Mercury 里的对话式界面，充当你的财务操作员。我一直在用 Command 转账、看我哪个类别花钱最多、分析现金流。就在今天，我用它查了过去一年某个赞助商给我赚了多少钱。我就问「过去一年我从 X 赚了多少？」10 秒后我就有答案了。太酷了。去 mercury.com 了解更多，几分钟在线申请。Mercury 是 FinTech 公司，不是 FDIC 受保银行。银行服务由 Choice Financial Group 和 Column N.A. 提供，FDIC 成员。(00:30:37)：好，回到产品领导力。你一路走来学到的东西，我们之前聊到你说过，你共事过的一些最好的产品 leader 更像策展人而不是有远见者。我想多听听这块。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, you do sometimes find amazing product leaders who are just idea machines, just prolific idea machines. But I do think a lot of the best have taste, have something about them that really makes really strong talent want to work with them, but end up sort of being curators, curators of people, curators of ideas, curators of technologies, curators of strategies. Because I don't really care if I'm hiring a strong lead for an area, if the strategy comes from them or comes from somebody else. I just care that there is an amazing strategy, and everyone has bought into it, and that we're executing against that strategy well. (00:31:39): And so I think that some of the best product leaders, yes, have ideas, it's hard to be a great curator if you don't have some of your own ideas, but embrace the reality that they can't come up with everything themselves, and so they need to create an environment in which great ideas bubble up and are chosen or decided upon. And so I think it's not just about curating ideas, but it's sometimes about curating teams and people.
turns.zh: 对。你确实有时会遇到那些就是 idea 机器、极其多产的 amazing 产品 leader。但我确实觉得很多最好的有品味、有某种让强人才想和他们共事的特质，但最终更像策展人——人的策展人、想法的策展人、技术的策展人、策略的策展人。因为如果我招一个强 leader 管一块业务，策略是他出的还是别人出的我不在乎。我在乎的是有没有一个 amazing 策略、大家都 buy in、我们在好好执行。(00:31:39)：所以我觉得一些最好的产品 leader，对，有 idea——如果你自己没点 idea 也很难做好策展人——但他们接受自己想不出所有东西的现实，所以需要创造一个让好 idea 浮现、被选中或被决定的环境。所以我觉得不只是策展 idea，有时也是策展团队和人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I so agree. I feel like everyone's always joining a team, and they just want to do vision strategy, just not actually hands-on work. "No AI's coming in here, let me do the strategy."
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。太同意了。感觉每个人加入团队都想做愿景策略，不想动手。「不，AI 来了，让我做策略。」

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love this point that there's so much power and value, and people underestimate just the need for just a really good curator of the team's ideas.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这一点：策展团队想法的需求被严重低估，这里有巨大价值和力量。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. Sometimes it's not just who's good or what idea's good. It's also what is going to work given the broader context. So for instance, on team building, a huge thing that I'm always considering is not just like, is this person a really strong candidate for this role? It is how does this person fit into their leadership team? So for an area like trust and safety, I have an engineering lead, I have a product staff lead, I have a data science lead, I have a design lead, I have a research lead. I need to make sure that those five compliment each other. And that's about what skills each one has, what weaknesses each one might have. (00:33:16): I also need to make sure that this is more art than science, have a good vibe. You need trust and rapport. A leadership team with strong trust and rapport can work through most anything. A leadership team without trust or rapport, anything can become an issue. And so that chemistry bit is, like I said, much more art than science. But that also matters. And so I think some of the best leaders and product leaders specifically also either do that instinctively or consciously, but they have a nose for building teams that are going to have good energy and good collaboration.
turns.zh: 对。有时不只是谁好或哪个 idea 好，而是在大环境下什么会 work。比如团队建设，我一直在考虑的不只是这个人是不是这个角色的强候选人，还有他在领导团队里怎么 fit。比如信任与安全这块，我有工程负责人、product staff 负责人、数据科学负责人、设计负责人、研究负责人。我要确保这五人互补。这关乎每个人有什么技能、有什么弱点。(00:33:16)：我还要确保——这更多是艺术而非科学——vibe 好。你需要信任和默契。一个有强信任和默契的领导团队几乎能扛过任何事。没有信任和默契的团队，任何事都能变成问题。所以那个 chemistry，如我所说，更多是艺术。但也很重要。所以我觉得一些最好的 leader，尤其是产品 leader，要么本能地、要么有意识地做到这一点，他们对能建出有好能量、好协作的团队有嗅觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Warm and fuzzy stuff.
turns.zh: 温暖而 fuzzy 的东西。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. Well, the flip side is also true. I've had many times in my career where I've had two people who I think are amazing, and I even adore them and love them, and they just can't get along. And you're like, "This isn't a competency issue. This is just a personality issue," and you just have to just sometimes call it, and split them.
turns.zh: 对。反面也一样。我职业生涯中有很多次，两个我都觉得很 amazing 的人，我甚至很喜欢他们，就是合不来。你就得说「这不是能力问题，是性格问题」，有时就是得叫停、把他们分开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to transition to talk about Instagram, the product, the platform, things you guys have learned there. Let me start with this question. What's something that the Instagram algorithm knows about human behavior that people may not realize?
turns.zh: 我想转到聊 Instagram 这个产品和平台，你们在那里学到的东西。先问一个问题：Instagram 算法对人类行为有哪些人们可能没意识到的了解？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: One of the most common misconceptions is actually in the opposite direction. I think people assume that there's a much more detailed semantic understanding of everybody's interests and preferences in the algorithm than there is. Most of what's really driven the progress in the world of recommenders over the last 5, 10 years have been these large embedding models and these other techniques that basically produce artifacts that cannot be read by people. They're not legible. They're giant vectors. It's like, sure, I can show you the vector, but it's just going to be a bunch of numbers in a seven-dimensional space. And so when we talk about, does the algorithm know something? Usually we think in these more semantic terms, it knows I like surfing. And it's like, "Eh." It doesn't. It just has this big-ass number that happens to correlate with surfing. (00:35:31): That said, I think that is starting to change. I think that one of the things that LLMs are enabling is they can describe in words, English or whatever language you prefer, what some of those previously-illegible artifacts are at least proximate to, if not mean directly. So this is like ... The thing I haven't really ... I posted about this this week, this thing called Your Algorithm. Basically the idea is we take a look at all of the stuff that you've interacted with, and then all of that is in an embedding space. You can think of embedding space as a map. You map a bunch of videos into the same map, and so videos that are close or similar. And now, we can just have an LLM just be like, describe that part of the map. And it can be like, "Oh, that is deep pour over coffee snobbery." And that's kind of amazing.
turns.zh: 最常见的误解其实是反方向的。我觉得人们以为算法对每个人的兴趣和偏好有非常详细的语义化理解，但实际上并没有。过去 5 到 10 年推荐系统领域的进步，主要来自大型 embedding 模型和其他技术，它们产出的东西人是读不懂的。不可读。是巨大的向量。就是，我可以给你看向量，但就是一堆七维空间里的数字。所以我们说算法「知道」什么时，通常用语义化的方式想——它知道我喜欢冲浪。但其实是「嗯」，它不知道。它只是有个巨大的数字恰好和冲浪相关。(00:35:31)：话虽如此，这开始变了。我觉得 LLM 能做到的一件事是，它们能用文字——英文或你偏好的任何语言——描述那些以前不可读的产物至少接近什么、甚至直接意味着什么。这就像……我还没完全……我这周发了关于这个的帖子，叫 Your Algorithm。基本想法是我们看你所有互动过的东西，所有这些在 embedding 空间里。你可以把 embedding 空间想成一张地图。你把一堆视频映射到同一张地图上，相近的视频就是相似的。现在我们可以让 LLM 描述地图的那块区域。它可以说「哦，那是深度手冲咖啡装逼」。这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so cool. You can ask the LLM to look at these numbers, and extrapolate here's the topic that you're interested in. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 这太酷了。你可以让 LLM 看这些数字，推断出你感兴趣的话题。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. Or look at the videos.
turns.zh: 对。或者看视频。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the videos.
turns.zh: 还有视频。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: And so the way you ... Both. You can also embed concepts into that same space. And so I mean, embeddings are really the underlying technology underneath LLMs. That's how all the whole thing works. (00:36:50): And so what we do now is we let you "see your algorithm." You can see what topics we think you're interested in and you can adjust it, you can add and remove things. But the idea here, giving people some agency back in a world where these social media apps are getting taken over by recommendations. But we can't do a lot of other things yet, but we will be able to do. There's things that aren't topical that you might ask for, "I want more fun content. I want to see my friends more. I don't want to see my high school's friends' kids' photos." I don't know, we can come up with a ... "I don't want to see seven photos in a row, but I'm happy to see six photos in a row." Whatever your mind can come up with. (00:37:36): So we have a lot of work to do, and so I'm excited about that. But I think a misconception historically is, until recently, we don't really know as much about you as you think. We're just like, "Oh, you liked these photos. These people also like those same photos, and they like these other photos, so you might like those other photos." I'm oversimplifying, but that's Kind of how it worked. Now, only now, are we actually getting as sophisticated as I think people have assumed we've been for many years.
turns.zh: 所以你……两个都行。你还可以把概念 embedding 到同一个空间里。embedding 其实是 LLM 底层的核心技术，整个东西就是这么运作的。(00:36:50)：所以我们现在做的是让你「看到你的算法」。你可以看到我们认为你感兴趣的话题，可以调整它、增删东西。这个想法是，在一个社交媒体 app 被推荐接管的世界上，给人一些 agency。但我们还做不了很多其他事，以后能做。有些不是话题性的，你可能要求「我要更多有趣的内容」「我要多看朋友」「我不想看我高中朋友孩子的照片」。我不知道，我们可以想出「我不想一次看七张照片，但六张可以」。你脑子里能想出的任何东西。(00:37:36)：所以我们还有很多要做，我很兴奋。但我认为一个历史性的误解是，直到最近，我们对你没你想的那么了解。我们就是「哦，你赞了这些照片。赞同样照片的人也赞这些其他照片，所以你可能也喜欢」。我过度简化了，但大致就是这样。现在，只是现在，我们才真正变得像大家以为我们已经很复杂的那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. One that comes to mind is this transition everyone eventually goes through to this algorithmic, broad global feed. It always feels, like people think, "I just want to see chronologically everyone I know and follow, and that's going to be my favorite feed," and it continues to be proven wrong. No, you actually engage a lot more when it's this algorithmic feed of things we think you will love.
turns.zh: 这真有意思。想到的一个是，每个人最终都会经历的向算法化、全球化 feed 的转变。大家总觉得「我就想按时间顺序看我关注的所有人，那才是我最喜欢的 feed」，但总被证明是错的。不，其实算法化 feed 推你我们会觉得你喜欢的内容时，你的参与度高得多。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, it's tough because ... I mean, I posted this week this thing about agency, and I just got destroyed in the comments, which is just part of the job. I get it. But there are a couple issues with the chronological feed. So one is ... And some of this is the tension between an individual's interests and what works when you scale it up. So if you do a pure chronological feed, the incentive for everybody is to just post as much as possible, because it will always be at the top of everyone who follows you's feed as soon as you post. So what ends up happening is that the feed gets overwhelmed with professional content, with usually large company content and publishers. The New York Times can pump out 50 things a day. Your best friend won't. You might get one thing a week from them. And so, your feed just gets taken over. (00:39:31): So part of it is the incentives that emerge, because when you design these systems, it's almost like designing a city. You need to think about, "Okay, here's how the mechanics work. What are the incentives that arise? How are people going to act within those incentives? And then what happens?" And the other thing is sometimes the most interesting thing was just not the most recent thing. Recency is an important input into relevance, but it's not the only one. My sister got engaged last night, and she's in Germany.
turns.zh: 对，这很难因为……我这周发了关于 agency 的东西，在评论区被喷惨了，这就是工作的一部分。我理解。但时间线 feed 有几个问题。一个是个人兴趣和规模化后的效果之间的张力。如果纯时间线，对所有人的激励就是尽可能多发，因为一发就在所有关注者 feed 的顶部。结果是 feed 被专业内容、通常是大公司和发布商的内容淹没。纽约时报一天能发 50 条。你最好的朋友不会。你可能一周才收到他一条。所以你的 feed 就被接管了。(00:39:31)：所以部分是涌现的激励，因为设计这些系统就像设计城市。你要想「好，机制是这样的，会涌现什么激励，人在这些激励下会怎么做，然后会怎样」。另一件事是有时最有趣的不是最新的。时间新鲜度是相关性的重要输入，但不是唯一。我姐姐昨晚订婚了，她在德国。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Congratulations.
turns.zh: 恭喜。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: No, she didn't. If she did. She's married. She got married last year. That's why it was top of mind.
turns.zh: 不，她没有。如果有的话。她已婚了。她去年结的。所以我才想到这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: But if she got engaged and I missed it because she lives in Europe and we're different time differences, do I really want to see a picture of my brother's po'boy sandwich, or do I want to see my sister's things first? (00:40:16): So it's tough. It's tough. I'd love to figure out a way to find the right balance. I want to give people agency over the experience, but I think it needs to be in a way that creates a system that makes sense. Not just for us as a business, which matters. I'm not pretending that's not an issue, but also for the overall community, because we've done chronological by default, or you can make a default, and you see not only does usage go down, overall sentiment goes down. The individual who made that choice might be happy at the moment, but when you just get pummeled with stuff you're less interested in over the course of months, we ask, we run surveys and massive scales. We just se people start to become less and less satisfied with Instagram.
turns.zh: 但如果她订婚了，因为时差我错过了，我是想看我哥的三明治照片，还是先看姐姐的事？(00:40:16)：所以很难。很难。我很想找到正确平衡的方式。我想给人对体验的 agency，但我觉得要在一个能创造合理系统的方式下。不只对我们作为生意——这很重要，我不假装这不是问题——也对整个社区，因为我们做过按时间线为默认，你可以设成默认，你看到不只是使用量下降，整体情绪也下降。做了那个选择的个人那一刻可能开心，但当你连续几个月被不那么感兴趣的内容轰炸，我们做大规模调研，就是看到人们对 Instagram 越来越不满意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of along these lines, everybody asks you about this these days, AI and content and how that all impacts everything that's going on. I want to ask you something I haven't seen someone ask you. Is the rise of AI content a headwind or a tailwind for Instagram versus other platforms? Do you think this helps or hurts you guys?
turns.zh: 差不多这条线，现在每个人都问你 AI 和内容以及它怎么影响一切。我想问一个我没见人问过你的：AI 内容的崛起对 Instagram 相对其他平台是逆风还是顺风？你觉得这帮你们还是害你们？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I think it's going to be a tailwind, but I think it's going to be a challenge. And not just because it's more content. Obviously, we're an attention-driven business. We're an advertising business. More content means potentially more attention. That's not for free, though. I don't think we're very good at ranking AI content yet. There's great AI content, this crap AI content. You should just see the stuff you're interested in and not any of the stuff you're not interested in. (00:41:40): But I do think that in a world where ... Or for years now, and I've said this many times, power shifting from institutions to individuals across industries. The easiest example of sports, where players are more relevant than teams now, and that was not the case when I was a kid. In that world, I think it behooves us to invest in individuals and to invest in, specifically, for Instagram and creators. And I mean creators broadly. I don't just mean influencers who are promoting branded content and making native-only videos. I mean, anybody who's using platforms like Instagram to help do what they do. You could be a journalist, you could be an artist, you could be selling scarves you sew. But you're out there, as yourself, creating and sharing content that helps you achieve whatever it is you're trying to do. (00:42:31): So we've been leaning in that direction for many years now. That's been one of our two or three most important audiences for as long as I've been on Instagram. In a world where there's an abundance of synthetic content, I actually think people are going to seek out creativity and authenticity and people more, not less. And I think that will help us. That doesn't mean that we won't have AI content on our platform. There's going to be bad and good AI content, and we're going to try and handle that the way we normally handle content. So unsafe goes away. Interesting versus not interesting is based on ranking and personalization. (00:43:08): But I think people are going to really seek out other points of view, because Instagram was never just about the content. It was always about, to a certain degree, the person behind the content, the point of view, the reason they're sharing it, their perspective. And I think that's going to become more important, not less. And I think given that we are not the best at a lot of things, but we are the largest creator platform. If you look at how we define creators and how many creators use us versus other platforms, I think it'll be a tailwind for us, because I think people are going to seek out people.
turns.zh: 我觉得会是顺风，但也会是挑战。不只因为有更多内容。显然我们是注意力驱动的生意、广告生意。更多内容意味着可能更多注意力。但这不是白来的。我覺得我们还不太擅长给 AI 内容排序。有好的 AI 内容，也有垃圾 AI 内容。你应该只看你感兴趣的，不看你不感兴趣的。(00:41:40)：但我确实觉得，在这个——我已经说了好几年——权力从机构向个人转移的世界里，最简单的例子是体育，现在球员比球队更重要，我小时候不是这样。在这个世界里，我觉得我们该投资个人、具体对 Instagram 来说投资创作者。我说创作者广义上，不只是推广品牌内容、做原生视频的网红。我是说任何用 Instagram 这类平台来帮助自己做事的人。可以是记者、艺术家、卖自己缝的围巾。你以自己的身份在那里，创作和分享内容来帮你实现你想做的事。(00:42:31)：所以我们很多年前就往这个方向倾斜。这是我上 Instagram 以来最重要的两三类受众之一。在一个合成内容泛滥的世界里，我反而觉得人们会更去寻找创意、真实性和人，不是更少。我觉得这会帮我们。这不意味着我们平台上不会有 AI 内容。会有好的和坏的 AI 内容，我们会试着像处理普通内容那样处理。不安全的下掉。有趣与否靠排序和个性化。(00:43:08)：但我觉得人们……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this connects to your earlier point that companies like, say, New York Times can pump out a bunch of AI content versus a creator. And so you're saying you kind of want to protect against that too, allow individuals to continue to perform well in spite of just all this AI content.
turns.zh: 这联系到你之前的点，像纽约时报可以批量产出 AI 内容而创作者不行。所以你也是说你想保护个人，让他在 AI 内容洪流中仍能表现好。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: If you just love AI content, great. You should be able to have a feed that's just AI town. And if you don't, then you shouldn't have it in your feed. To me, it's like ... I don't think we should ... I understand why people are. I'm not oblivious to the overall paradigm shift and sort of revolution that we're sitting in. But I don't think we should judge content based on the tool that made it. I think we should judge it based on the content, the point of view, the person behind the content. I don't think we should filter out AI content. I think we should let you know if content is AI content or not. I think we should let you know more about the person who posted anything, so that you can make informed decisions about whether or not to believe or trust them based on knowing who they are, or where they are, or how many times they've changed their profile, or if their profile's three days old or three years old. But I don't think we should be making value judgements based on what tool you used.
turns.zh: 如果你就是爱 AI 内容，很好。你应该能有一个纯 AI 小镇的 feed。如果你不喜欢，那你的 feed 里就不该有。对我来说就像……我不觉得我们该……我理解为什么大家这么想。我不是没看到我们身处的范式转变和革命。但我不觉得我们该根据制作工具来评判内容。我觉得该根据内容本身、观点、内容背后的人来评判。我不觉得我们该过滤掉 AI 内容。我觉得我们该让你知道内容是不是 AI 的。我觉得我们该让你更多了解发任何内容的人，这样你能基于知道他是谁、在哪、改过几次资料、资料是三天还是三年，来做出是否相信他的明智决定。但我不觉得我们该根据你用了什么工具做价值判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an AI content creator you love that you're just like, "This is so good. I love watching these AI videos."
turns.zh: 有没有一个你喜欢的 AI 内容创作者，就是「这太好了，我爱看这些 AI 视频」？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. What is she called? Plastic Dream Sequence. Is that what it is?
turns.zh: 有。她叫什么来着？Plastic Dream Sequence。是这个吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. [inaudible 00:45:12] check it out.

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Check it out, yeah. Plastic Dream Sequence. I have it on my phone. I'll double check. It's these sort of dolls, Barbies, but they're singing songs in these little tiny silhouettes and snippets. And it's just amazing. It's a little weird, but also kind of amazing. And it's very clearly AI, it's not pretending not to be, but it has a very clear creative and aesthetic point of view. And every time I come by one, I'm like, "Yep, we're doing this now." I'm going to watch this for 30 seconds.
turns.zh: 看看，对。Plastic Dream Sequence。我手机上有。我确认一下。就是那种娃娃、芭比，但它们在唱一些小片段的歌。太棒了。有点怪，但也有点 amazing。很明确是 AI，没装不是，但有非常清晰的创意和审美观点。每次我刷到，我就「对，我们现在就是做这个」。我要看 30 秒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have it pulled up here, and I want to watch it, but I'm not going to. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 我这里搜出来了，我想看但不看。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Ifonly.ai, that's another one. He's in France. I think he's in Paris. He uses multiple different tools and models, but he kind of tries to create these dreamscapes and animate them. So he uses one model to create the image, another one to create the video, music, et cetera. He's very clearly got his own aesthetic. And you could think of him as a painter, but this is his tool.
turns.zh: Ifonly.ai，另一个。他在法国，好像在巴黎。他用多种工具和模型，但基本是创造这些梦境并让它们动起来。一个模型做图，另一个做视频、音乐等等。他有自己明确的审美。你可以把他看作画家，只是这是他的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a vision of AI versus human in the feed? Do you think it'll... You said you maybe want to mark it. How do you think about people? Are they going to be like AI account, not AI count? How do you think about it, or is that still kind of a work in progress?
turns.zh: 有没有 AI vs 人类在 feed 里的设想？你觉得它会……你说你可能要标注。你怎么想？会不会有 AI 账号、非 AI 账号？你怎么想，还是说还在进行中？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Maybe we'll end up in the same place, but there's a difference between marking content and marking accounts, and they're both useful and interesting. So if content was created with AI, I think you should be able to know that. That's hard, by the way, because we can detect that right now, but as these models get better, we might lose the ability to detect that. So we should also be very careful to be honest with you about how confident we are in our own sort of assessment. (00:46:56): But I think you should be able to just ask, be like, "Hey, is this AI?" And we should be able to tell you who we think it probably is, or we're not sure, or it's definitely not, or it definitely is. I actually think we might be more practical to label camera captured content, basically non-AI content as opposed to labeling AI content long-term for a couple of reasons. (00:47:17): But then at the account level, I think it also matters. There's definitely a new spam vector, which is these fake accounts. Which by the way, an AI creator, that's fine. There's nothing wrong with that necessarily. But there are these spam vectors which are trying to abuse that, and they're selling bogus supplements, and it's like an AI monk, and it doesn't present it, and it's not obvious that it's an AI, and it's just trying to take advantage of a certain aesthetic or a certain sort of stereotype. We need to figure out how to crack down on that. And so I do think we should be making sure that you know. Basically you just need to know, and then you can make your own informed decision. Is the account a real person or not? Is the content a real piece of content or not?
turns.zh: 也许我们最终会到同一个地方，但标注内容和标注账号是两回事，都有用、都有意思。如果内容是 AI 创作的，我觉得你应该能知道。这很难，顺便说，因为我们现在能检测，但随着模型变好，我们可能会失去检测能力。所以我们也要对自己有多大把握非常诚实。(00:46:56)：但我觉得你应该能直接问「嘿，这是 AI 吗？」我们应该能告诉你我们觉得大概是、不确定、肯定不是、肯定是。其实我觉得更实际的是标注相机拍摄的内容——即非 AI 内容——而不是标注 AI 内容，长远来看，有几个原因。(00:47:17)：但在账号层面，我觉得也重要。确实有新的垃圾信息向量，就是这些假账号。顺便说，AI 创作者没问题，没什么不对。但有这些滥用它的垃圾向量，卖假保健品，是个 AI 和尚，不标明，不明显是 AI，就是利用某种审美或刻板印象。我们得想怎么打击。所以我确实觉得我们该确保你知道。基本你就是需要知道，然后自己做明智决定。账号是不是真人？内容是不是真的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you think about other platforms in the space, social content platforms, are there any features or ways of approaching stuff that they do well, that you're kind of jealous of or really impressed by?
turns.zh: 当你想这个领域的其他平台、社交内容平台，有没有什么功能或做事方式他们做得好，你有点嫉妒或很佩服的？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, there's a bunch. So many people do so much. I mean, for me, one of the things that we are finally catching up with, but I've been always very impressed with is TikTok and their recommenders' ability to break small talent. In the world of ranking and recommenders, you can talk about exploitation-based ranking. That sounds terrible, but it just means using the data you have. And then you can talk about exploration-based ranking, going and trying to figure out what someone might be interested in, that they might even not know they're interested in yet. And it is much easier to move engagement by showing people stuff that you know they'll probably like because lots of people like it. It's much harder to go and figure out how to essentially test content so that we can see, "Hey, sure you like Bieber, but you might also like Afropunk. And so we're just going to show you some Afropunk and see what happens." (00:49:12): If you do the latter, this exploration-based ranking, I think it's really good for niche creators and small creators, because you give them a chance to find an audience that either wasn't going to see on them before or didn't even know that they were interested before. So we've invested a lot over the last couple of years in ranking, not just increasing engagement, but increasing originality, increasing the number of pieces of content that break out, increasing recency to stay culturally relevant. And so a lot of that has been inspired by TikTok and ByteDance. (00:49:44): I think we're catching up. There's actually a couple of those areas where we, I think, by best we can tell, we're ahead of them. There's a couple where we're still behind. But we have line of sight to, I think, being the best-in-class at recommendations for the first time during my tenure. So I think they get a lot of credit for inspiring a lot of that work.
turns.zh: 有，有很多。很多人做了很多。对我来说，我们终于追上但一直很佩服的是 TikTok 及其推荐系统发掘小人才的能力。在排序和推荐的世界里，你可以谈基于利用的排序——听起来很糟，就是用你有的数据。然后是基于探索的排序，去试你可能会感兴趣、甚至你自己还不知道会感兴趣的。用你知道他大概会喜欢的东西来提升参与度容易得多，因为很多人喜欢。去试内容、发现「你喜欢 Bieber，但你也可能喜欢 Afropunk，我们就给你看点 Afropunk 看看」难得多。(00:49:12)：如果你做后者——探索性排序——我觉得对小众创作者和新人特别好，因为你给他们机会找到以前看不到、甚至不知道自己感兴趣的受众。所以过去几年我们在排序上投了很多，不只是提升参与度，也提升原创性、提升能突围的内容数量、提升时间新鲜度以保持文化相关。很多是受 TikTok 和字节跳动启发。(00:49:44)：我觉得我们在追上。有几个领域我们尽所能判断已经领先。有几个还在后面。但我们第一次在我任期内看到了成为推荐领域 best-in-class 的路径。所以我觉得他们在启发这些工作上功不可没。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nice job.
turns.zh: 干得好。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Well, we'll see. Not there yet. They call me disappointed dad. My team is always like, "Can you ease up on the disappointed dad vibe?" So I'm trying to be a little bit more generous about giving people their flowers.
turns.zh: 嗯，走着瞧。还没到。他们叫我「失望老爹」。我团队总是说「你能稍微收一下失望老爹的 vibe 吗？」所以我试着更慷慨地给人肯定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like you say that, but that's an interesting common thread across really successful leaders, is just never being satisfied. Always feeling-
turns.zh: 你这么说，但这其实是个有趣的成功领导者的共同点——永不满足。总觉得——

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, it's a blessing and a curse.
turns.zh: 对，是祝福也是诅咒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... here's all the problem. It is. Yeah. (00:50:35): On this creator piece, I think that's also ... People complain about this global algorithm not showing them all their friends, but I feel like this is a benefit of what happens when you do this, now that you can break new creators into a wide audience if you have this kind of global algorithmic feed, which is really great for a lot of people.
turns.zh: ……这都是问题。确实。(00:50:35)：关于创作者这块，我觉得这也是……大家抱怨全球算法不给他们看朋友，但我觉得这就是全球算法化 feed 的好处——你能把新创作者推向广大受众，对很多人很好。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I mean, I'm out there talking about a lot of these contentious issues, and I get beat up a lot in the comments, which is fine. My main thing here is just to try to communicate that there's almost always trade-offs. You can't just have all of the things, unfortunately. You want to never see something you're not interested in, then you're also just going to see the most basic, general, lowest-common denominator stuff all the time. You want to discover new and interesting things? You're occasionally going to see stuff that was just a miss. But this isn't just true about ranking. All these major debates have trade-offs. Privacy and safety. Those two things are in contention. Do you want a company scanning your messages or not? There's some really significant trade-offs on both sides of that debate. (00:51:47): And so generally speaking, when I argue and engage in debate with people who feel really strongly about things, I'm not usually trying to convince them. Their mind is usually made up. I'm just trying to enumerate all of the different puts and takes for the rest of the people watching the conversation.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我在外面谈这些有争议的事，在评论区被喷很多，没关系。我主要想传达的是几乎总有取舍。你不幸不能要所有东西。你永远不想看到你不感兴趣的，那你就只会一直看最基础、最大众化的东西。你想发现新鲜有趣的，偶尔就会看到不合适的。但这不只是排序。所有这些大辩论都有取舍。隐私和安全，这两者是对立的。你要不要公司扫描你的消息？这场辩论两边都有非常重大的取舍。(00:51:47)：所以一般来说，当我和对某事有强烈观点的人辩论时，我通常不是在试图说服他们。他们主意已定。我只是在为看这场对话的其他人列举所有取舍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of getting torn apart in the comments, you are so in the middle and thick of all of these really hairy situations, changing the feed, you were in the Cambridge Analytica lawsuit, all this. You're in the center of so much controversy. Is that ... You're like, "Yep." Oh, man. Is that just like you, "I will lean into this. This is the thing I need to do." Or is it Zuck being like, "Adam, you got to be the front face of all the stuff, and get in there." Where does that come from?
turns.zh: 说到在评论区被撕，你处在所有这些棘手情况的中心——改 feed、Cambridge Analytica 诉讼……你在太多争议的中心。那是……你就「嗯」。天哪。是你自己「我要冲上去，这是我该做的」？还是 Zuck 说「Adam，你得做这些事的前台」？这从哪来？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: It started on newsfeed. So I used to run newsfeed on Facebook, and my take was that the debate was going to happen with or without us, so we might as well participate. And so I started being really active on Twitter specifically, because that's where journalists really lived at the time, and I thought it would show some humility to show up on their turf, so to speak. My Twitter ended up being the darkest place in my life because I just followed all of our biggest critics. That's not a dig on Twitter. That was just what I did. And that's where it started, and it kind of slowly built from there. (00:53:15): For better or for worse, we've become a really important part of daily life for a lot of people. We touch a lot of people, we have a lot of responsibility, and there's a lot of change. And with change means there's going to be anxiety and stress and scrutiny. We've made great decisions, we've made mistakes. We've been criticized for things that I think ... We've been criticized unfairly, we've been criticized fairly. And so we just need to accept that this debate is going to happen broadly. So I just think it's better for us to talk about it, and just be clear about what we're doing, why we're doing it, what the trade-offs are. If people disagree, that's okay. We're not necessarily winning over friends when we talk about what we do. But I think over the long run, people are fundamentally more afraid of things that they don't understand and about things where people are more secretive and less accessible. (00:54:09): And so I've tried to show up in an accessible and authentic way, and I've made mistakes, and I have enjoyed it at times, and hated it at other times. But that's kind of how it started. There was also a fun debate in Mark's senior leadership team a long time ago, where we were just talking about how we're a social media company, but we had a very sort of conventional approach to communication and press releases, and say, "Why don't we just use our platform?" So I was not in that debate, but I stuck myself into that debate trying to mediate it. But that was also a reason why I ended up getting sucked in because Mark was like, "All right, well, let's see. Why don't you try and see how it goes?"
turns.zh: 它从 newsfeed 开始。我以前管 Facebook 的 newsfeed，我的看法是辩论有没有我们都会发生，所以不如参与。我开始特别活跃在 Twitter 上，因为那时记者主要在那里，我觉得去他们的地盘能显示一些谦逊。我的 Twitter 后来成了我生活中最黑暗的地方，因为我关注了所有我们最大的批评者。这不是说 Twitter 不好，只是我那么做的。就是从那开始的，然后慢慢壮大。(00:53:15)：无论好坏，我们成了很多人日常生活里很重要的一部分。我们触达很多人，有很多责任，也有很多变化。变化意味着焦虑、压力和审视。我们做过好决策，也犯过错。被不公平地批评过，也被公平地批评过。所以我们需要接受辩论会广泛发生。我觉得不如我们去谈，说清楚我们在做什么、为什么、取舍是什么。如果人们不同意，没关系。我们谈我们做的事时不一定赢得朋友。但长远来看，人们本质上更害怕他们不理解的东西、和人更保密、更不可及的东西。(00:54:09)：所以我试着以可及、真实的方式出现。我犯过错，有时享受、有时讨厌。但它就是那么开始的。很久以前在 Mark 的高管团队里也有过有趣的辩论，我们说我们是社交媒体公司，但沟通方式很传统、发新闻稿，为什么不直接用……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that helps you deal with the hate that flows at you every time you say something that people disagree with?
turns.zh: 有什么能帮你应对每次你说别人不同意的话时涌来的恨意？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: You try to put it in perspective. So it started with ... I did the redesign of newsfeed in 2009. We launched it March of 2009 for Facebook. I was a designer, I was an IC designer, front entry-level designer. And the first comment that came in was something pretty derogatory. I think it was homophobic and antisemitic. Literally, we're all sitting there. We launched this thing, and we're just looking at the stream of comments, and it's the first one. And it was specifically about ... They don't know me, but it was like, "What exploitive expletive censor censor designed this shit?" And I was like, "Oh, it was me." (00:55:43): And I was devastated. I was like a 25-year-old kid. And, I don't know, I thought about it, and I came to this idea that if you spent 30, 40, 50 minutes a day at your desk, and you organized your photos there, and you wrote letters to your friends there, and you read there, and then I just came, and I rearranged your desk, and I didn't tell you, I didn't warn you, I didn't even explain why, you would be pissed, and that would be reasonable. And that was what was happening just with millions of people. (00:56:17): So I tried to put things in perspective, and then I tried to step away from it, get time with my kids, get time outside. There are months where it's really not hard at all and there are months where it really, really grinds on me.
turns.zh: 试着把它放进视角。最早是……2009 年我做 newsfeed 改版。2009 年 3 月在 Facebook 上线。我是设计师，IC 设计师，入门级。第一条评论就挺贬损。好像恐同又反犹。真的，我们所有人坐在那，上线这个东西，看着评论流，第一条。具体是说「哪个剥削性的 xxx 设计了这坨屎？」而我在想「哦，是我。」(00:55:43)：我崩溃了。我才 25 岁。后来我想了想，得出一个想法：如果你每天在桌前待三四十分钟，在那整理照片、给朋友写信、阅读，然后我来把你的桌子重新摆了，没告诉你、没预警、甚至没解释为什么，你会很生气，那是合理的。这就是发生在数百万人身上的事。(00:56:17)：所以我试着放进视角，然后试着抽离，和孩子待会，去户外。有几个月完全不难，有几个月真的很煎熬。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, there was a famous kind of reversal when you redesigned the feed into this kind of video scroll-y experience. There's this whole protest. The world protested.
turns.zh: 说到这个，有一次著名的反转——你把 feed 改成视频滚动体验。全世界抗议。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah, that was pretty rough.
turns.zh: 对，那次挺惨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was kind of like, "Okay, wow, we're actually not right, and we should go back."? What helped you decide, "Okay, let's change course."?
turns.zh: 什么样的时刻让你觉得「好吧，我们其实不对，该回去」？什么帮你决定「好，改方向」？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: So actually that one, three or four things got conflated. We had to redesign a feed that went to the video viewer. That was a test to 4% of users on iOS. It was not going to roll out. It was just an early test to get us some sense and feedback on the idea. We were also leaning into Reels a lot. We were also leaning into recommendations, so posts from accounts you don't follow, a lot. And there were also creators who were upset about the fact that their reach was going down, and they were blaming ranking changes on that. (00:57:22): Those four things got all conflated. We had some pretty big-name creators publicly slap us. Then the press covered that creator sort of backlash, which then got more creators doing it. So we ended up with this little bit of like a multiplier effect or echo between the creator community and the press back and forth. But we were never going to launch that. That was an early test. We knew it needed to work. We actually have continued to grow video, and invest in creative tools, and invest in ranking, and invest in recommendations, and that's driven most of our growth in the years since.
turns.zh: 其实那次是三四个事被混在一起了。我们改了 feed 进视频查看器。那是面向 4% iOS 用户的测试。不会全量推出。只是早期测试获取反馈。我们当时还在大力做 Reels。也在大力做推荐——你没关注的账号的帖子。还有一些创作者因为 reach 下降而不满，怪排序变化。(00:57:22)：这四件事被混在一起。一些大创作者公开打我们。然后媒体报导了创作者的反弹，又带动更多创作者这么做。所以我们有了创作者社区和媒体之间来回的乘数效应或回声。但我们从来没打算上线那个。那是早期测试。我们知道它需要 work。其实我们后来继续增长视频、投资创作工具、投资排序、投资推荐，这驱动了我们之后几年的大部分增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Showed them.
turns.zh: 让他们看看。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: I think we were pushing ... Well, I don't know. It doesn't feel like ... I think my real takeaway wasn't that we should have not tested that design necessarily. I think we could have done a bunch of things better to explain, and maybe move a little slower. I think we were just pushing things a little bit too fast. And when you are responsible for a platform like Instagram, you need to be reasonable and realistic about how much you can evolve it. (00:58:31): Now, I would much rather have backlashes like that every couple years, but continue to evolve and continue to stay relevant than the alternative, which would've been like we didn't have video, we didn't have DMs, we didn't have Stories, we didn't have ranking. And we wouldn't be having this podcast right now. But the cost of leaning in is that you're going to occasionally make a mistake and you're going to definitely pay for it.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们在推……嗯，我不知道。不觉得……我真正的 takeaway 不是我们不该测那个设计。我觉得我们本可以在解释上做得更好，也许慢一点。我觉得我们只是推得太快了。当你负责 Instagram 这样的平台，你需要对能演进多少保持合理和现实。(00:58:31)：不过，我宁愿每两年有那种反弹但持续演进、保持相关，也不要另一种——没有视频、没有 DM、没有 Stories、没有排序。那我们现在也不会有这期播客。但拥抱的代价是偶尔会犯错、肯定会付出代价。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how running experiments now is very risky for companies at your scale. One person spots it, and I go, "Shit."
turns.zh: 有意思的是，在你这个规模跑实验现在很有风险。有人一发现，就「糟糕」。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Kind of need to have a ... You don't need to be proactive about communicating it, but you need to have a comm strategy. For any design change or any test that could be controversial, we talk about it beforehand and be like, "Okay, not if it leaks, when it leaks, what are we saying? Should we talk about it proactively? Should we talk about it reactively? Either way, what's the message?" Because you can't launch something to three billion people and not test it first, but you can't test something at our scale and not expect people to cover it. And so you have to be ready to talk about it before you even know you want to launch it. So it makes the development cycle more complicated than it used to be.
turns.zh: 基本需要有……你不需要主动沟通，但需要有 comm 策略。对任何设计变更或可能有争议的测试，我们事先就谈「好，不是如果泄露，是何时泄露，我们说什么？要不要主动谈？要不要被动回应？不管哪种，message 是什么？」因为你不能对 30 亿人上线不测，但也不能在我们这个规模测试不预期有人会报导。所以你甚至在你确定想不想上线之前就得准备好谈它。这让开发周期比以前复杂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The head of growth at Anthropic launched an experiment with pricing, and it just went crazy on Twitter. He's like, "It's rolled out to 1% of people. We're just [inaudible 01:00:02]." They're like, "No, Anthropic. Come on."
turns.zh: 对。Anthropic 的增长负责人搞了个定价实验，在 Twitter 上炸了。他说「只对 1% 的人推出了。我们只是[听不清 01:00:02]。」大家说「不，Anthropic，别这样。」

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Pricing particularly, that one is a real ... You got to be real careful with that one. We've all learned these lessons. We should all share notes more, that's what I think.
turns.zh: 定价尤其，那个是真的……得非常小心。我们都学过这些教训。我们应该多交流笔记，我觉得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "Here's not what to do." How to avoid the internet hating you for the day.
turns.zh: 「别这么做。」如何避免被互联网恨一天。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Yeah. I'm happy to talk to that [inaudible 01:00:18] in Anthropic.
turns.zh: 对。我很乐意和 Anthropic 那位[听不清 01:00:18]聊聊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think he's all right. He's all right. (01:00:22): Okay, I'm going to take us to two recurring corners on the podcast, Fail Corner and Hot Seat Corner. Fail Corner, what's something that you worked on that was just a huge failure that helped you become better?
turns.zh: 我觉得他没事。他没事。(01:00:22)：好，我要带你进入播客两个 recurring corner，Fail Corner 和 Hot Seat Corner。Fail Corner：你做过什么是巨大失败、但帮你变得更好的？

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: Oh, a bunch.
turns.zh: 哦，很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many.
turns.zh: 这么多。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: So I'll give you two maybe. So before Instagram, my first project as a PM was on a project called Facebook Home, which was a sort of fork of Android at the operating system level-
turns.zh: 我给你两个。在 Instagram 之前，我作为 PM 的第一个项目叫 Facebook Home，是 Android 在操作系统层面的一个 fork——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember that.
turns.zh: 我记得那个。

turns.speaker: Adam Mosseri
turns.en: ... and a piece of hardware with HTC. It was a spectacular failure. I learned way more in that year, year and a half than I did in any year, I think, probably in my career, because I was just a design manager before that.
